Obstinacy is the quality of stubbornly refusing to change your opinion, decision, or behavior — even when there are very good, clear reasons to do so.

Think of it this way: imagine someone has made up their mind about something. People show them solid evidence that they are wrong. Friends reason with them. Experts advise them. And yet, that person will not budge — not even a little. That quality — that hardened, immovable refusal to reconsider — is obstinacy.

It is not just being firm. It is being unreasonably, almost defiantly firm.

This is a negative word. When you call someone's behavior "obstinacy," you are not complimenting them. You are saying their refusal to change is not justified — that a reasonable person, faced with the same facts, would have reconsidered by now.

The word carries a sense of frustration. It suggests:

  • The person is aware of the reasons to change, but ignores them.
  • Their stubbornness is making things worse.
  • Others have tried, and failed, to get through to them.

A doctor tells a patient: "You must stop eating so much salt — your blood pressure is dangerously high."

The patient says, "I've eaten this way my whole life. I'm not changing now."

The doctor explains the risks again. The family begs him. His test results worsen. Still, he refuses.

His refusal to change, despite all the evidence and pleading, is obstinacy.
How It Is Used in a Sentence

• "His obstinacy frustrated everyone on the team — he refused to consider a single suggestion."
  • "Despite the setbacks, she pushed forward with obstinacy that bordered on recklessness."
  • "The negotiations failed because of the obstinacy of both sides."
  • "The child's obstinacy in refusing to eat vegetables drove his parents to despair."

Obstinacy is not only used to describe people. It can also describe situations, problems, or conditions that resist change or refuse to improve.

For example:

  • "The obstinacy of the infection surprised the doctors — no antibiotic seemed to work."
  • "The obstinacy of the stain meant it wouldn't come out no matter how hard she scrubbed."

Here, "obstinacy" is used almost as if the thing has a stubborn will of its own. It just won't yield.
The Crucial Difference: Obstinacy vs. Determination

These two are easily confused, so this distinction matters.

Determination is admired. It means you pursue a worthy goal with strong willpower even when things get hard. The resistance is external — the world is pushing back, but you keep going. People cheer you on.

Obstinacy is criticized. It means you cling to an opinion or behavior even when logic, evidence, or wise counsel says you should change. The resistance is internal — your own mind refuses to move. People grow frustrated with you.

The key question is: Is the refusal to change reasonable, or not?

If yes → you are being determined, principled, or resilient.
If no → you are displaying obstinacy.
Closely Related Words (and How They Compare)

Stubbornness is the closest synonym. It means almost exactly the same thing and is used more casually in everyday speech. Obstinacy is slightly more formal and often implies an even stronger, more deep-seated refusal.

Inflexibility is broader — it simply means an inability or unwillingness to adapt. Obstinacy specifically involves actively resisting when pushed to change.

Intransigence is a more formal, often political synonym — it describes someone who flatly refuses to negotiate, compromise, or come to an agreement.

Mulishness and pig-headedness are informal, colorful synonyms that emphasize how irrational or animal-like the stubbornness is (as a mule is famously difficult to move).
The opposites are words like flexibility, open-mindedness, compliance, and tractability — all of which describe a willingness to listen, adapt, and change when good reasons exist.

Obstinacy is the quality of stubbornly and unreasonably refusing to change your opinion or behavior, even when faced with compelling evidence, sound advice, or strong persuasion — and this refusal is seen by others as unjustified and frustrating.
